President of Russia Vladimir Putin: Good evening.

I suggest we skip opening remarks and go straight to your questions. Please.

Question: Good evening, Mr President.

Nikita Korzun, NTV.

Your trilateral meeting with Xi Jinping and Donald Trump looks absolutely historic. But do you think it was historic in essence? What did you discuss, and what will happen next?

Thank you.

Vladimir Putin: Nobody knows what will happen next. Only God knows that.

However, I would really want it to have a continuation, at least because in terms of comparing notes, in a number of key areas, we have reached if not an agreement, then a mutual understanding.

This primarily concerns its historical significance and the like. There have never been such meetings before. We have held the first meeting, which has opened a new page in the history of diplomacy.

As for what we discussed, by and large, the topics of our meeting did not differ much from those raised at the plenary session. However, since our three countries are permanent members of the UN Security Council, we talked about its reform, a possible reform of the UN and about increasing its potential. All of us agree that this should be done, and that the operation of this universal organisation should be adjusted to modern realities.

We talked about security matters in the broad sense of the word, about preventing the proliferation of weapons of mass destruction, nuclear weapons. We talked about issues pertaining to freedom of navigation. We support compliance with all norms of the international law of the sea. We discussed some issues related to the activities of certain organisations, such as the International Criminal Court, which is clearly overstepping its mandate and making political rather than legal decisions. By and large, all sides are in agreement on that.

We also discussed several other issues. You know, what I liked about that meeting, and what made an extremely positive impression on me, is that after we made our official statements, which we prepared in advance, in the presence of media representatives and your colleagues, we held an open discussion. I even think that none of us expected that. However, the President of China, who initiated this meeting, managed to create an atmosphere in which we freely exchanged views on several issues of mutual interest. It was probably the most interesting element of the meeting. Our discussion was held in a completely open and very candid atmosphere. It helped us understand each other better, and I think that this created conditions for future arrangements, no matter whether we do this in the same or in a different format. Overall, it was a very useful meeting.

Question: Good evening. Pavel Zarubin, Rossiya TV channel. You have known Mr Trump for nearly ten years now. We first saw the two of you meet at the G20 summit in Hamburg in 2017. Those meetings were typically followed by major, significant statements, yet they yielded no real results, often leading only to new sanctions instead. Even during Mr Trump’s second term, after the meeting in Anchorage too, the situation has been, to put it mildly, far from straightforward. In your view, is the current United States even capable of reaching agreements, and would they actually honour such agreements if they were to be concluded?

Vladimir Putin: You know, we are watching the situation closely. Members of the media, your colleagues who cover politics, are analysing this too, and they can see that the domestic political situation in the United States, and the country’s political system itself, is far from simple; one might even say it is rather complex. There are many checks and balances in place – various mechanisms designed to maintain a balance of political power. So, from the outside, things might appear inconsistent or not quite how we would like them to be.

But the most important point is this – and I have no doubt about it – President Trump is genuinely committed to resolving conflicts, including the conflict in Ukraine, and he is sincerely interested in improving bilateral relations across a range of areas, including, of course, the US-Russia relationship, which matters to us.

Naturally, we are observing developments. Of course, we would prefer to see things move faster and function more effectively. But we must deal with realities as they are, and we hope that this positive disposition will endure.

I mentioned this during our recent discussions in a multilateral format, and I can repeat it now. After all, we did work with President Trump during his first term. We did not work with him afterwards, once he left the presidency in 2020. Yet, both then and now, we share certain commonalities in our approaches – specifically regarding what are termed “civilisational values.” In that sense, there is something that, if not exactly uniting us, at least points to a certain alignment of views.

For instance, we were just discussing the issue of democracy – but what is democracy, really? Is it the liberal order that certain groups have sought, and continue to seek, to impose upon the entire world, fashioned according to their own template? Is that what democracy is? Or is it, in fact, a liberal attempt to monopolise power, a liberal dictatorship? What is it, exactly?

Reaching a common denominator – let alone fully implementing any agreements reached – is no simple task. Nevertheless, the general resolve of those we are engaging with today gives us reason to maintain a positive outlook. It is better to have some form of agreement, even if it is not fully realised, than to have no agreement at all.

Question (retranslated): Spasibo, Mr President.

I am Zou Yun, with China Media Group.

Regarding this historic meeting with President Xi and President Trump, what is the issue, or the issues, that you believe have achieved the greatest progress? And how do you understand the significance of the four proposals put forward by President Xi for global major powers to work together and save our global peace? And also, how would you describe the role of China in achieving those outcomes?

Thank you, Mr President.

Vladimir Putin: In this instance, China’s role has been decisive, as it was President Xi Jinping who initiated this meeting, which has clearly been a success. I would like to reiterate that this was largely because the President of the PRC succeeded in creating a relaxed setting for an open discussion. Furthermore, he set the tone for this frank exchange, in that he acted not only as the host of the meeting itself but also as the one who suggested having this open dialogue. In my view, this is very important as it lays the groundwork for further engagement – not only for the exchange of information, but also for preparatory work on certain decisions, perhaps in a different format. But this format is, in my view, timely and successful, given, as I have already mentioned, that China, Russia and the United States are permanent members of the United Nations Security Council and, as such, international security depends to a considerable extent on us.

Therefore, I would like, firstly, to congratulate the President of the PRC on the success of his event, which proved highly productive, and secondly, to thank him for his initiative. I am confident that all the issues – and I have just named the topics that were tabled for discussion – were addressed promptly, and the very fact that they were discussed, and that common ground was found in order to resolve them, is undoubtedly positive.

Question: Anastasia Savinykh, TASS News Agency.

Mr President, have our starting positions at the talks on European security become tougher than the proposals you advanced in 2021, which the West rejected? Will we demand any compensation from the West for the damage caused to Russia because of sanctions and strikes on our infrastructure with Western weapons? Is there any consensus on the territorial issue and ceasefire, or have the negotiations on this track hit a stalemate?
